lesson.title: Mobile IP: Keeping One Address While Your Network Changes Under You
lesson.summary: Mobile IP lets a device keep a single permanent IP address as it moves between networks, using a home agent, a temporary care of address, and tunneling to bridge the gap between a fixed identity and a moving location.
lesson.body:
Every device on the internet is expected to sit at a fixed IP address that routers can use to find it, but a phone or laptop moving between networks breaks that assumption constantly. Mobile IP, standardized for IPv4 in RFC 2002 and its successors, solves this by giving a mobile node a permanent home address that never changes, no matter which physical network it joins, so that any application holding an open connection to that address keeps working through the move.

The mechanism rests on three pieces. A home agent sits on the mobile node's home network and keeps track of where the device currently is. When the device moves onto a foreign network, it acquires a temporary care of address, either assigned by a foreign agent on that network or obtained directly, and registers that care of address with its home agent. From that point forward, any packet sent to the mobile node's permanent home address arrives at the home agent first, which wraps it inside a new IP header addressed to the current care of address, a process called IP in IP encapsulation or tunneling, and forwards it. The foreign agent, or the device itself, strips the outer header back off on arrival so the original packet looks untouched to the application that sent it.

This design deliberately separates two jobs an ordinary IP address tries to do at once: identifying who a device is, and describing where it currently sits on the network. The home address handles identity, the care of address handles location, and the tunnel between the home agent and the current care of address is what lets the identity stay fixed while the location changes underneath it. Without that separation, every time a device joined a new network it would need a new IP address, and every open TCP connection tied to the old address would break the moment the device moved.

Mobile IP has a well known inefficiency called triangle routing: traffic from a correspondent host always passes through the home agent first, even if the mobile node has moved right next door to the correspondent, because the correspondent only ever addresses packets to the home address. Route optimization extensions let a correspondent learn the current care of address directly and skip the home agent, but the base protocol accepts the detour as the price of keeping addressing simple.

Mobile IP is a network layer solution and is conceptually distinct from the link layer handoff a phone performs when it moves from one cell tower to another on a cellular network; a handoff keeps a device attached to the radio network as it moves, while Mobile IP keeps a device reachable at a stable IP address once the radio layer has already reconnected it somewhere else. In practice, cellular networks rarely use classic Mobile IP today, since packet core architectures like the LTE Evolved Packet Core handle mobility internally, but the ideas of a home address, a care of address, and tunneling reappear throughout mobile networking wherever a stable identifier has to be decoupled from a device's changing point of attachment.
